en: Such, indeed, is this worthless world.
My elder had met the infidel’s bullets
And found himself cast
Into the very embers of hell.
The noble hero had fallen
Into the hands of the merciless.
The eagle hero was caught
In the enemy’s inescapable net
And seemed to have fallen headlong
Into a boiling pit of Chinese troops.
Seeing this, brave Seytek thought:
“If fate has caught me, let me die;
But if God grants me another day beyond death,
Against these fierce-armed warriors,
Against this dreadful enclosing net,
Against the champions displaying their strength
And this host relying on sheer numbers,
Let me unleash a great tumult.
I shall whirl my spear and break their ranks;
If my days are done, I shall fall to a bullet.
If the Creator’s decree
Descends upon my head, I shall face it.
To my elder, left to me by my forefathers,
To that mountain-like shelter,
Let me become a companion.”
So saying, brave Seytek advanced,
His cry splitting heads,
His shout splitting stones,
Like an ember that scorched the eyelashes,
Coiled to strike like a dragon.
The forty holy guardians and Khidr-Ilyas
Raised their cries and shouted his battle call,
Surging from every ridge:
“Charge, Seytek, charge!”
The guardian saints who took him by the hand
Clamored from every side
And leveled their spears in line.
Companions appeared from the unseen world
And served as protectors
To the noble lion’s son.
A lion strode before him
As though ready to rend its prey,
Prancing in terrible majesty.
One of the holy guardians, a gray tiger,
Crawled ahead of him.
A mighty-limbed leopard,
A black-mottled prince,
Bore the terror of a thousand men.
Striding fiercely at his flank,
He kept ill-fated Seytek
Within the line and guided him forward.
Another, clad in iron armor and shield,
Led him by the hand:
“If you act, act like this;
If you slaughter the foe, slaughter them so.”
Another surged ahead,
Calling, “Seize that enemy!”
On every side rose a mighty din,
As his supporters spoke.
Where the hero above them
Heaved forward in a wave,
No mountain could have withstood him;
If he poured out his rage in one place,
No Chinese force could match him.
Long-bodied and broad-shouldered,
That noble, strong-boned lion,
Who made every confronting foe submit,
That noble son of a valiant hero,
Was like a towering plane tree in a tangled forest,
Clearing a road as he advanced.
Ninety-four armed enemies stood together,
Led by the fortunate Chongbilgich.
He attacked Chongbilgich,
Throwing all ninety-four into confusion.
He urged on the gray horse, huge as a mountain,
Making it stride proudly
And gallop with bounding steps.
Kulansur loomed like a mountain
As the champion waging holy war
Plunged once more into the fray.
He struck Kulansur once upon the thigh
And cried aloud, “Akjoltoy!”
His extended spear was a burning ember;
Fury boiled and his soul blazed,
And he valued his life no more than a hair.
Does not a hero die for honor?
Does not this borrowed, fleeting soul behold
What Almighty God has ordained?
If He demands this life,
Must it not be given, whenever the hour?
When fate claims this head,
Where is a night like the sacred Night of Power?
Against the infidels who came by choice,
Against the warriors who fixed their hatred on me,
Let me test myself in battle.
Let a man be seen by his enemy;
For the land where his cord was cut,
For the people who openly sustained him,
Let the champion’s blood be spilled.
Better than every worldly blessing,
Best and noblest of all,
Is for a hero to die by an enemy’s hand.
Shall they plunder and scatter
The wealth of the teeming people,
And let the enemy trample the land
Where our cords were cut and our swaddling washed?
Rather than lose our champions and break our strength,
Rather than let the people be pillaged,
Let me face the frenzied foe.
To my doomed elder Joltoy,
To the sheltering figure who protected us—
When I see him, my heart is shocked,
Yet at the sight of him my heart finds peace.
Let me witness upon the open steppe
The ruin of all ninety-four.
If God ordains it and opens the way,
For my elder who has suffered torment,
For my forebear who knows my worth,
Let me become a shield.
There is an ancient saying:
For solid iron there is a hammer,
For the forlorn there is God;
Where there are eyes, grass will grow,
And the earth will swallow the tyrant.
They attacked my people living freely,
And tirelessly raided my herds.
Accursed sons who have renounced their mothers,
They tore my sleep open like scattered entrails,
Scattered my possessions over the hills,
And drove my people to distraction.
The wretched Chinese have made
My elder Joltoy, my lake of strength, waste away.”
His battle cry split heads.
When Akjoltoy looked across,
The figure of Seytek
Appeared before his eyes.
When he saw brave Seytek,
His blood surged and raced,
And his beloved protector came into view.
Strength entered him; grinding his teeth,
The doomed man said:
“My protector has come—so be it!
If I now die at the hands
Of a warrior mighty in terror, my heart is content.
My valiant one has appeared before my eyes;
If I die now, I have no regret,
Not the smallest regret remains in me.
If I should die suddenly,
If by chance my time has come,
There is one who will seize and fold me at the waist,
One I trust as my support,
Who will load me for the journey to Ala-Too.
He will not let the beasts devour me,
Nor let it be said that Joltoy died
At the hands of the merciless.
He will not harbor dreadful thoughts,
Nor let wolves tear flesh from my haunches,
Nor allow the fanged beasts
To dishonor my soul in the end.
‘Dig and turn the earth with a mattock—
Seytek has come, bury me,’” he said.
Placing his hope in the young man,
He was wholly freed from anxiety;
No longer fearing the Chinese calamity,
His spirits lifted and his heart grew calm.
“My protector has visibly come;
As I depart this world,
I have seen my beloved one,” he thought.
Taking heart, he braced himself.
Seeing the gray wolf, Akjoltoy
Counted that lone hero as a host;
His anguish subsided,
And hope in his fleeting life returned.
His sorrowful heart relaxed,
And Joltoy stood watching.
He saw a broad-chested figure,
Seeming like a bridge across a mighty river,
Guarding all the people.
That falcon born a champion,
Whose fathers and forefathers
Had never retreated before an enemy,
Tightened and buckled his war belt,
Then attacked the ninety-four.
A roar of shouting rose before him;
The valor of the young champion blazed
As he invoked his ancestors in his battle cry:
“In this holy war,
Support me, my own heroic father!
My forefather Manas the lion,
Make straight the path before me now!”
Upon his mountain-like gray horse,
In his billowing golden coat,
He poured out his wrath, grim-faced.
The gray war belt inherited from his forefathers
Blazed brightly, fastened around his waist.
Like a prince ruling a nation,
He rejoiced when he saw the champion,
Like a man beholding at her wedding feast
His maiden beloved, the beautiful Bermet.
His mighty teeth, broad as a gate,
Showed within his mouth,
While blue smoke thick as an arm
Streamed from the corners of his lips.
Charging downhill, the hero speared
The ninety-four who met him;
Among the Chinese who pressed upon him,
Each bore the fury of a thousand,
Each was a black demon incarnate,
Yet he skewered them two at a time.
Of the forefathers who had gone before,
Which one could have struck more fiercely?
He made Kulansur prance,
And laid low all who faced him.
Those he grappled with he never released;
Some of those champions
Could never be filled though feasts were cooked,
And once they fought, they spared no life.
Their prowess surpassed all others;
They stood foremost before the khan,
Champions of deadly venom.
Swearing to devour the Burut whole,
They had made their pledge firm
And readied every piece of armor.
Of the warriors who came from Beijing,
No fewer than fourteen giants lay dead;
The Chinese advance was cut off.
As the battle raged on,
Chongbilgich roared aloud,
Thundering and surging into fury.
He was said to be the son of Kün-Jangjung,
And they called him Küpü the Wrestler.
He was immensely strong in a grapple;
When he seized a man in combat,
He would twist and break his neck.
He could overturn a mountain in his path
And uproot anyone he encountered;
If a man fled, he never escaped.
He confronted all whose death had come.
His prowess was renowned:
“He is the son of Ai-Jangjung,
This is the warrior from Beijing
Destined for the khan’s golden throne,”
So it was entered in his record.
“He is the greatest of forty tribes;
The misery of every enemy
Who meets him will boil without end.”
His valor was well known;
Clairvoyants in Beijing
And judges of men had tested him.
His nose was like a mountain spur;
He drew breath like a dragon,
As though he could devour the entire world.
His eyes were blue as steel;
When you looked upon his nose,
It resembled a ridge where a rich lord camped.
